plan.topic: How to check whether a GLP-1 pharmacy is legitimate: the FDA's BeSafeRx red flags, the NABP pharmacy-licence lookup, and how FDA-approved, compounded and counterfeit semaglutide and tirzepatide differ
plan.angle: Title (60 characters or fewer): 'Semaglutide or Tirzepatide Online: How to Check a Pharmacy'. Thumbnail: 'Real Pharmacy?' next to a labelled, curious pharmacist character. The S3 CTA must use this exact title. Body: 0–15 s, the dated FDA recall notice as the hook, then the answer: 'a legitimate pharmacy needs a prescription, is state-licensed and has a US pharmacist you can reach'. Sections are chapters named as questions people search. (a) The FDA BeSafeRx signs, quoted word for word. (b) How to check a licence with your state board of pharmacy or the NABP. (c) Approved vs compounded vs counterfeit, in 60–90 s: compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and the FDA does not review them for safety, effectiveness or quality before they're sold; counterfeits are fakes. Then the three FDA counterfeit Ozempic alerts with their dates. (d) 'Research use only' means not for people. (e) Report to FDA MedWatch, or the MHRA Yellow Card in the UK. Common GI side effects of the approved medicines, one line. 'Don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own.' The full prescriber line. End by naming one already-published Lane B long-form.
plan.working_title: Is My GLP-1 Pharmacy Legit? What the FDA Says to Check
plan.why: First Lane B long-form this week. It runs on the strongest Short lane (median 102), uses a searched-phrase title of 60 characters or fewer, and rests on stable FDA and NABP primary pages rather than breaking news. | fact-check: A Lane B evergreen topic with real search demand. The structure is safe and nothing in it explains how to buy. Problems to fix: (1) The hook. As far as I can find, the Oct 21, 2026 USA Today story is a nationwide recall of 22 compounded tirzepatide vials from a pharmacy the FDA warned in Dec 2025. We already ran a compounded tirzepatide recall Short (10-20 S1) and a 'compounded vs counterfeit' Short. The 14-day no-repeat rule means the recall can only be a hook of 15 seconds or less, the compounded-vs-counterfeit part must stay a short section, and the core of the video is pharmacy checks. Credit the recall to the FDA or the company notice, not to USA Today alone. (2) The title names no drug. Our data shows drug-less titles fail, and Lane A/B rules want the searched phrase plus the generic name first. (3) Quote the BeSafeRx red flags word for word from the current FDA BeSafeRx page, with its last-reviewed date: requires no valid prescription, no US state-licensed pharmacist available, not licensed by the state board of pharmacy, prices dramatically lower, no physical US address. Don't paraphrase them. (4) Counterfeit Ozempic alerts I confirmed on fda.gov: Dec 2023 (lot NAR0074, serial 430834149057), Apr 2025 (lot PAR0362, serial starting 51746517) and Dec 2025 (counterfeit 1 mg, lot PAR1229, which is also a real lot number; the EXP/LOT text sits to the left instead of above). Cite each from its own FDA page with its date. (5) If the video uses the claim that about 95% of online pharmacies operate illegally, credit it to the NABP with the report year, or cut it. (6) Present NABP and state-board lookups as ways to verify, not as endorsements. Never show a pharmacy's name or URL on screen.

package.description:
How to check an online pharmacy for semaglutide or tirzepatide, step by step.

Quick answer: a legitimate pharmacy requires a valid prescription, is licensed by your state board of pharmacy, and has a state-licensed pharmacist you can reach. The FDA warned about counterfeit Ozempic in the U.S. supply chain in Dec 2023, Apr 2025 and Dec 2025, and a lot number alone isn't proof. Even genuine medicines have side effects; the most common are gastrointestinal, like nausea.

General information, not personal advice. Don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
FDA counterfeit Ozempic alerts: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fda-warns-consumers-not-use-counterfeit-ozempic-semaglutide-found-us-drug-supply-chain
FDA BeSafeRx FAQs: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/besaferx-your-source-online-pharmacy-information/besaferx-frequently-asked-questions-faqs
FDA on unapproved GLP-1 drugs: https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fdas-concerns-unapproved-glp-1-drugs-used-weight-loss
NABP Boards of Pharmacy: https://nabp.pharmacy/about/boards-of-pharmacy/

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

scenes.section: Can you trust an online GLP-1 pharmacy?
scenes.narration: One thing first: this is general information, not personal advice. Your prescriber is the right person for decisions about your treatment.

scenes.section: What are the FDA's warning signs?
scenes.narration: The FDA runs a consumer campaign called BeSafeRx, built for exactly this moment: buying medicine online.

visual.stock_query: FDA shield over laptop shopping cart

scenes.narration: BeSafeRx says a safe online pharmacy will do four things. Here they are, close to the FDA's own wording.

scenes.narration: One: require a prescription from a licensed health care professional.

scenes.section: What are the FDA's warning signs?
scenes.narration: Two: be licensed by your state board of pharmacy.

scenes.narration: Three: have a state-licensed pharmacist available to answer your questions.

visual.stock_query: woman raising eyebrows, two red flags

scenes.section: What are the FDA's warning signs?
scenes.narration: Quick reality check, though. An online doctor visit isn't a red flag by itself. A legitimate telehealth service still has a licensed prescriber assess you, and the prescription goes to a licensed pharmacy.

scenes.section: What are the FDA's warning signs?
scenes.narration: But here's the problem. A slick website can copy a logo, list an address and post a phone number. So how do you check what's real?

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?
scenes.narration: This is the part most people skip, and it's free. You can check a license yourself, in a few minutes. These steps are for the U.S. Outside the U.S., check with your own country's pharmacy regulator.

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?
scenes.narration: Step one: your state board of pharmacy. The FDA's BeSafeRx campaign says checking a pharmacy's license through your state board is an important step.

visual.stock_query: state capitol building with pharmacy sign

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?
scenes.narration: Don't know where your board is? The National Association of Boards of Pharmacy, or NABP, keeps a list of every state board, with links.

visual.stock_query: map of US with pharmacy icons

scenes.retention_device: Answers the viewer's next question before they ask

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?
scenes.narration: On your board's website, look for the license search. Type in the pharmacy's name, and look for an active pharmacy license.

visual.stock_query: person typing in search box, focused

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?
scenes.narration: Step two: NABP's consumer site, safe dot pharmacy. You can type in a website address and see whether NABP has reviewed it, including whether it's on their 'not recommended' list.

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?
scenes.narration: Step three: look at the web address itself. NABP runs the dot pharmacy domain, and only approves it for websites that meet its standards.

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?
scenes.narration: One important caveat. These lookups verify, they don't endorse. A license tells you someone is accountable. It doesn't tell you which pharmacy is cheapest or right for you, and we never recommend any seller.

visual.myth: A license lookup recommends a pharmacy
visual.stock_query: scales balancing license and question mark

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?
scenes.narration: Step four is the human test. Call, and ask to speak with the pharmacist. The FDA's list says a safe pharmacy has a state-licensed pharmacist available to answer your questions.
scenes.retention_device: Human, simple test the viewer can do today

scenes.section: How do I check a pharmacy's license?

scenes.section: Compounded vs counterfeit: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: Online, three very different things can all be called semaglutide or tirzepatide. Let's separate them in under a minute.

visual.stock_query: three labelled boxes side by side

scenes.section: Compounded vs counterfeit: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: First, FDA-approved medicines: brands like Ozempic and Wegovy for semaglutide, Mounjaro and Zepbound for tirzepatide. The FDA reviewed them for safety, effectiveness and quality before they could be sold.

scenes.section: Compounded vs counterfeit: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: Second, compounded versions. The FDA is direct about this: compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and the FDA does not review them for safety, effectiveness or quality before they're marketed.

visual.fact: Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved or FDA-reviewed before sale

scenes.section: Compounded vs counterfeit: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: Compounding has legitimate uses, through a licensed pharmacy with a prescription. But it isn't the approved medicine. If you're offered a compounded version, ask your prescriber what that means for you.
scenes.retention_device: Agency: a question to bring to the doctor

scenes.section: Compounded vs counterfeit: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: Third, counterfeit. That's a fake, made to look like the real thing. The FDA warns counterfeit medicines may contain the wrong ingredient, too much or too little active ingredient, none at all, or other harmful ingredients.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete risks make the category vivid

scenes.section: Compounded vs counterfeit: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: And here's what surprises people. Counterfeits don't only turn up on shady websites. Which brings us back to those three FDA alerts, and the twist.
scenes.retention_device: Surprise + callback to the opening loop

scenes.section: What does 'research use only' mean?

factcheck.summary: I checked every factual claim in the script against its source, and they hold up. On the three counterfeit Ozempic alerts, the FDA page confirms the dates (12/21/2023, 4/14/2025 and 12/5/2025), lot NAR0074 with serial 430834149057, lot PAR0362, and the counterfeit needles in the 2023 alert. It also confirms the twist in the open loop: in December 2025, lot PAR1229 on the 1 mg pens was a real lot number used on genuine pens, Patient Assistance Program pens with that lot are authentic, and the fakes have the EXP/LOT text to the left instead of above. The FDA's advice in s44 is a near-exact match for its own wording. The four signs of a safe pharmacy and the red flags match the BeSafeRx FAQ (current as of 09/21/2020), and the 'important step' line matches the FDA's license-lookup page. The compounding quote matches the FDA's unapproved GLP-1 page (10/01/2026), and the counterfeit-contents list matches the Counterfeit Medicine page. Patients can report to MedWatch directly, and suspected counterfeit products are listed as reportable. The UK Yellow Card scheme accepts reports of both side effects and fakes. NABP's site lists the state boards, its safe.pharmacy tool covers 'Not Recommended' websites and .pharmacy domains (confirmed by search, because the page blocks automated access), and the side-effect lists match MedlinePlus. The safety pieces are in place: the 'not personal advice' line (s09, s70), the prescriber line (s69), the don't stop, switch or change line (s58), a named common side effect, no seller named, no dosing, and gray-market buyers pointed to a prescriber. Jen is clearly presented as imagined. The title is fully paid off. There are two small wording fixes below.

issues.claim: Severe stomach pain that doesn't go away needs medical attention right away.
issues.problem: MedlinePlus describes the warning sign as ongoing stomach pain that won't go away and may spread to the back, with or without vomiting. It doesn't say 'severe'. Adding 'severe' narrows the warning, so a viewer could think pain that keeps going but isn't severe is fine to ignore.
issues.fix: Narration: "Stomach pain that won't go away, which may spread to your back, with or without vomiting, needs medical attention right away." On-screen text: "Stomach pain that won't go away? Get help". List item 4: "Stomach pain that won't go away: get help now".

issues.claim: The FDA reviewed them for safety, effectiveness and quality before they could be sold.
issues.problem: The cited page (fda_concerns) only says that compounded drugs are not reviewed. It never says this directly about approved drugs. The claim is true in general, but the source tag doesn't say the line it's attached to.
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "The FDA reviewed them before they could be sold. That's the step compounded versions skip." Keep source_ids ["fda_concerns"]. On-screen text can stay "1. FDA-approved: reviewed first".

thumbnail.reasoning: Candidate #1 ('SPOT THE FAKE') has the clearest single focal point, strong emotional contrast (a worried/sad fake pen vs. a happy approved pen), explicit labels that remove ambiguity, and no visual defects. Candidates #0 and #2 both show the same unfinished-looking blank white placeholder box on the stop-sign mascot, which reads as a rendering/QA bug and undercuts polish and trust on a medical-safety video. #2 also has a small, multi-line subhead that will be hard to read at a glance in the phone feed. #1's headline stays under the 4-word limit, doesn't repeat the title, and pays off the video's 'how to check' promise honestly without overstating it.
